claim: Exercise-induced cognitive improvements have traditionally been observed following aerobic exercise interventions.
source: Exercise-induced cognitive improvements have traditionally been observed following aerobic exercise interventions; that is, sustained sessions of moderate intensity.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: A 6-week high-intensity training (HIT) regimen was tested on measures of cognitive control and working memory in a multicenter, randomized (1:1 allocation), placebo-controlled trial.
source: Here, we tested the effect of a 6 week high-intensity training (HIT) regimen on measures of cognitive control and working memory in a multicenter, randomized (1:1 allocation), placebo-controlled trial.
evidence: This describes the study design and methodology.

claim: 318 children aged 7-13 years were randomly assigned to a HIT or an active control group matched for enjoyment and motivation.
source: 318 children aged 7-13 years were randomly assigned to a HIT or an active control group matched for enjoyment and motivation.
evidence: This describes the sample size and randomization procedure.

claim: The 6-week HIT regimen resulted in improvements on measures of cognitive control with BFM = 3.38, g = 0.31 (0.09, 0.54).
source: The 6-week HIT regimen resulted in improvements on measures of cognitive control [BFM = 3.38, g = 0.31 (0.09, 0.54)]
evidence: Statistical results from the study showing effect on cognitive control.

claim: The 6-week HIT regimen resulted in improvements on measures of working memory with BFM = 5233.68, g = 0.54 (0.31, 0.77).
source: The 6-week HIT regimen resulted in improvements on measures of cognitive control [BFM = 3.38, g = 0.31 (0.09, 0.54)] and working memory [BFM = 5233.68, g = 0.54 (0.31, 0.77)]
evidence: Statistical results from the study showing effect on working memory.

claim: The cognitive improvements from HIT were moderated by BDNF genotype, with met66 carriers showing larger gains post-exercise than val66 homozygotes.
source: The 6-week HIT regimen resulted in improvements on measures of cognitive control [BFM = 3.38, g = 0.31 (0.09, 0.54)] and working memory [BFM = 5233.68, g = 0.54 (0.31, 0.77)], moderated by BDNF genotype, with met66 carriers showing larger gains post-exercise than val66 homozygotes.
evidence: Statistical results showing genetic moderation of training effects.

claim: Individuals with higher cardiovascular fitness typically show higher performance on a wide range of cognitive measures, from cognitive control to working memory and executive functioning.
source: Individuals with higher cardiovascular fitness typically show higher performance on a wide range of cognitive measures, from cognitive control (Pontifex et al., 2011) to working memory (Erickson et al., 2013) and executive functioning (Colcombe and Kramer, 2003; Hillman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Long-term sport practice is associated with higher working memory capacity.
source: In addition, long-term sport practice is associated with higher working memory capacity (Moreau, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Long-term sport practice is associated with spatial ability.
source: In addition, long-term sport practice is associated with higher working memory capacity (Moreau, 2013), spatial ability (Moreau, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Long-term sport practice is associated with more efficient visual processing of movements.
source: In addition, long-term sport practice is associated with higher working memory capacity (Moreau, 2013), spatial ability (Moreau, 2012), and more efficient visual processing of movements (Güldenpenning et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Greater fitness indices have been linked to differences in white matter integrity.
source: In neuroimaging studies, greater fitness indices have also been linked to differences in white matter integrity (Chaddock-Heyman et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: Greater fitness indices have been linked to larger hippocampal areas.
source: In neuroimaging studies, greater fitness indices have also been linked to differences in white matter integrity (Chaddock-Heyman et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2013), as well as with larger hippocampal (Weinstein et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: Greater fitness indices have been linked to larger cortical areas.
source: In neuroimaging studies, greater fitness indices have also been linked to differences in white matter integrity (Chaddock-Heyman et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2013), as well as with larger hippocampal (Weinstein et al., 2012) and cortical areas (Erickson et al., 2009; Makizako et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: Physically fit individuals show increased long-term potentiation (LTP) in the visual system compared to the non-fit.
source: These results are corroborated by increased long-term potentiation (LTP) in the visual system of physically fit individuals compared to the non-fit (Smallwood et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: LTP plays a primary role in major cognitive processes such as learning and memory.
source: a key finding given the primary role of LTP in major cognitive processes such as learning and memory (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993, Bliss and Lomo, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational research on LTP.

claim: Exercise interventions can elicit cognitive improvements in diverse populations ranging from children to the elderly.
source: Exercise interventions can elicit cognitive improvements in diverse populations ranging from children (Davis et al., 2011) to the elderly (Fabre et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous intervention studies.

claim: Exercise interventions can elicit cognitive improvements in individuals with various clinical conditions such as developmental coordination disorders and schizophrenia.
source: Exercise interventions can elicit cognitive improvements in diverse populations ranging from children (Davis et al., 2011) to the elderly (Fabre et al., 2002), as well as in individuals with various clinical conditions such as developmental coordination disorders (Tsai et al., 2012) and schizophrenia (Pajonk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous intervention studies in clinical populations.

claim: Exercise-induced cognitive improvements appear to be dose-dependent.
source: Furthermore, improvements appear to be dose-dependent (Davis et al., 2007; Vidoni et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Exercise-induced cognitive improvements are not restricted to atypical or clinical populations—adults at their cognitive peak show similar benefits.
source: Furthermore, improvements appear to be dose-dependent (Davis et al., 2007; Vidoni et al., 2015), and are not restricted to atypical or clinical populations—adults at their cognitive peak show similar benefits (Gomez-Pinilla and Hillman, 2013; Moreau and Conway, 2013; Voss et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In school settings, exercise interventions have been shown to be associated with higher levels of academic achievement.
source: In school settings, exercise interventions have shown to be associated with higher levels of academic achievement (Coe et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Exercise regimens in children typically lead to improvements in various aspects of cognition, including executive function, cognitive control and memory.
source: exercise regimens in children typically lead to improvements in various aspects of cognition, including executive function, cognitive control and memory (see for a review Tomporowski et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Interventions implemented in early stages of life allow capitalizing on higher cortical plasticity, potentially maximizing their impact.
source: Interventions implemented in early stages of life allow capitalizing on higher cortical plasticity, potentially maximizing their impact (Cotman and Berchtold, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and draws on knowledge about developmental plasticity.

claim: Sibley et al. found a robust effect of physical exercise on cognitive function in children, in a meta-analytic assessment of the literature.
source: Consistent with these findings, Sibley et al. found a robust effect of physical exercise on cognitive function in children, in a meta-analytic assessment of the literature at the time (Sibley and Etnier, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: Most studies evaluating the impact of exercise on cognition have evaluated aerobic exercise.
source: Most studies in this line of research have evaluated the impact of a rather specific type of regimen, based on aerobic exercise.
evidence: This is a general observation about the literature, based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Aerobic exercise is usually defined as a sustained regimen performed at moderate intensity.
source: Usually defined as a sustained regimen performed at moderate intensity (e.g., McArdle et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: Aerobic exercise has come to be accepted as the form of exercise typically associated with neural changes and cognitive enhancement.
source: aerobic exercise has come to be accepted as the form of exercise typically associated with neural changes and cognitive enhancement (Hillman et al., 2008; Thomas et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Current exercise interventions are rooted in early findings in the animal literature, which typically investigated the effects of physical exercise in rodents—animals who naturally favor aerobic forms of exercise.
source: First, current interventions are rooted in early findings in the animal literature, which typically investigated the effects of physical exercise in rodents—animals who naturally favor aerobic forms of exercise (Gould et al., 1999; Shors et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal research and draws on knowledge about rodent behavior.

claim: The most dramatic gains in cognition from exercise have been observed in the elderly.
source: Second, the most dramatic gains in cognition have been observed in the elderly (Erickson et al., 2015; but see also Etnier et al., 2006; Young et al., 2015, for a more nuanced view)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research, with acknowledgment of nuance.

claim: Moderate-intensity exercise is seemingly most adequate for the elderly population.
source: the most dramatic gains in cognition have been observed in the elderly (Erickson et al., 2015; but see also Etnier et al., 2006; Young et al., 2015, for a more nuanced view), a population for which moderate-intensity exercise is seemingly most adequate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the elderly population and exercise research.

claim: Regimens based on resistance training have shown sizeable effects on cognition.
source: For example, regimens based on resistance training have shown sizeable effects on cognition (Best et al., 2015; Liu-Ambrose et al., 2012; van Uffelen et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of improvements from resistance training are potentially different from those elicited by aerobic exercise.
source: regimens based on resistance training have shown sizeable effects on cognition (Best et al., 2015; Liu-Ambrose et al., 2012; van Uffelen et al., 2007), despite underlying mechanisms of improvements being potentially different from those elicited by aerobic exercise (Goekint et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: More complex forms of motor training that combine high physical and cognitive demands appear encouraging for cognitive improvement.
source: More complex forms of motor training that combine high physical and cognitive demands also appear encouraging (Moreau et al., 2015; Tomporowski et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Interventions based on short, intense bursts of exercise can induce physiological changes that mirror those following aerobic exercise on a wide variety of outcomes.
source: Moreover, a compelling body of research in the field of exercise physiology indicates that interventions based on short, intense bursts of exercise can induce physiological changes that mirror those following aerobic exercise on a wide variety of outcomes.
evidence: This is a general statement about research findings in exercise physiology.

claim: High-intensity training (HIT) can induce physiological changes in measures of cardiovascular function.
source: These include measures of cardiovascular function (Chrysohoou et al., 2015; Gayda et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High-intensity training (HIT) can induce physiological changes in overall fitness.
source: These include measures of cardiovascular function (Chrysohoou et al., 2015; Gayda et al., 2016), overall fitness (Benda et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: High-intensity training (HIT) can induce physiological changes in general health.
source: These include measures of cardiovascular function (Chrysohoou et al., 2015; Gayda et al., 2016), overall fitness (Benda et al., 2015), and general health (Milanović et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In some cases, physiological improvements following high-intensity training (HIT) can even go beyond those typically following aerobic regimens.
source: In some cases, physiological improvements following high-intensity training (HIT) can even go beyond those typically following aerobic regimens (Rognmo et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HIT appears to be particularly effective to increase the release of neurotrophic factors essential to neuronal transmission, modulation and plasticity—potentially surpassing aerobic exercise regimens.
source: For example, HIT appears to be particularly effective to increase the release of neurotrophic factors essential to neuronal transmission, modulation and plasticity—potentially surpassing aerobic exercise regimens (Ferris et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Short bouts of exercise have been shown to alleviate some of the difficulties typically associated with Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children.
source: Short bouts of exercise have been shown to alleviate some of the difficulties typically associated with Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children (Piepmeier et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The benefits of short bouts of exercise reported in the Piepmeier et al. study were not limited to children diagnosed with ADHD—typical children also exhibited cognitive improvements.
source: The benefits reported in this study were not limited to children diagnosed with ADHD, however—typical children also exhibited cognitive improvements.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from the cited Piepmeier et al. study.

claim: Pontifex and colleagues found that a single 20 min bout of exercise was sufficient to improve cognitive function and scholastic performance in children.
source: More strikingly perhaps, Pontifex and colleagues found that a single 20 min bout of exercise was sufficient to improve cognitive function and scholastic performance in children (Pontifex et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Exercise-induced cognitive improvements typically occur after longer training periods.
source: This is an impressive finding, given that exercise-induced cognitive improvements typically occur after longer training periods (Etnier et al., 2006; Sibley and Etnier, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Short-term improvements immediately following acute bouts of exercise typically dissipate after a few hours.
source: Importantly, these effects should be distinguished from short-term improvements immediately following acute bouts of exercise (Tomporowski, 2003), which typically dissipate after a few hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The hypothesized mechanisms for short-term consequences of single acute exercise sessions involve heightened state of alertness induced by neurotransmitter increases.
source: The hypothesized mechanisms are, however, different—heightened state of alertness induced by neurotransmitter increases for the former (Tomporowski, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The hypothesized mechanisms for more durable benefits from exercise involve slower but more durable neurophysiological adaptations.
source: The hypothesized mechanisms are, however, different—heightened state of alertness induced by neurotransmitter increases for the former (Tomporowski, 2003), and slower but more durable neurophysiological adaptations in the case of the latter (Erickson et al., 2011, Erickson et al., 2015; Moreau and Conway, 2013; Voss et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The studies by Piepmeier et al. and Pontifex et al. utilized regimens of moderate intensity—a reported 62–72% and 65–75% of individual maximum heart rate, respectively.
source: Although focused on short sessions, the aforementioned studies utilized regimens of moderate intensity—a reported 62–72% (Piepmeier et al., 2015) and 65–75% (Pontifex et al., 2013) of individual maximum heart rate, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Based on findings from the physiological literature, there are clear mechanisms via which exercising at a high intensity could influence cognition in a meaningful manner.
source: Yet based on findings from the physiological literature (e.g., Rognmo et al., 2004), there are clear mechanisms via which exercising at a high intensity could influence cognition in a meaningful manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and draws on knowledge of physiological mechanisms.

claim: HIT could elicit improvements above and beyond those typically following short sessions of moderate intensity, and provide a legitimate, time-efficient alternative to longer aerobic exercise regimens.
source: Arguably, HIT could elicit improvements above and beyond those typically following short sessions of moderate intensity, and provide a legitimate, time-efficient alternative to longer aerobic exercise regimens (Costigan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential of HIT, supported by a citation.

claim: The conjunction of promising early findings and clear mechanisms of action has prompted discussions to implement HIT interventions more systematically within the community.
source: Together, the conjunction of promising early findings and clear mechanisms of action has prompted discussions to implement HIT interventions more systematically within the community (Gray et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Several studies have investigated the role of specific genetic polymorphisms on the magnitude of exercise-induced improvements.
source: In an effort to better understand and predict individual responses to physical exercise interventions, several studies have investigated the role of specific genetic polymorphisms on the magnitude of exercise-induced improvements (Erickson et al., 2008, Erickson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Many studies have focused on the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) val66met polymorphism, given its direct influence on serum BDNF concentration.
source: Among these, many have focused on the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) val66met polymorphism, given its direct influence on serum BDNF concentration (Lang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: BDNF is known to support neuronal growth and has been shown to facilitate learning.
source: BDNF is known to support neuronal growth and has been shown to facilitate learning, a process that in turn induces BDNF production (Berchtold et al., 2001; Cotman and Berchtold, 2002; Kesslak et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Learning induces BDNF production.
source: BDNF is known to support neuronal growth and has been shown to facilitate learning, a process that in turn induces BDNF production (Berchtold et al., 2001; Cotman and Berchtold, 2002; Kesslak et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The dynamic coupling between BDNF and learning makes BDNF an important underlying factor of exercise-induced cognitive improvements.
source: This dynamic coupling makes BDNF an important underlying factor of exercise-induced cognitive improvements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between BDNF and learning.

claim: It has been proposed that individuals whose particular BDNF polymorphism is associated with lower activity-dependent BDNF levels (met66 carriers) might benefit from exercise interventions to a greater extent than individuals whose activity-dependent BDNF levels are higher (val66 homozygotes).
source: Consistent with this idea, it has been proposed that individuals whose particular BDNF polymorphism is associated with lower activity-dependent BDNF levels (met66 carriers) might benefit from exercise interventions to a greater extent than individuals whose activity-dependent BDNF levels are higher (val66 homozygotes).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous research and knowledge of BDNF polymorphisms.

claim: A few studies have shown that individuals with lower cardiovascular function might maximize benefits from physical exercise interventions designed to improve cognitive function.
source: Similarly, a few studies have shown that individuals with lower cardiovascular function might maximize benefits from physical exercise interventions designed to improve cognitive function (Sofi et al., 2011; Strong et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The implicit assumption is that although lack of physical exercise might be a limiting factor for individuals whose fitness level is low, more active individuals might be less impacted by an exercise intervention program.
source: The implicit assumption is that although lack of physical exercise might be a limiting factor for individuals whose fitness level is low, more active individuals might be less impacted by an exercise intervention program (Heyn et al., 2004; Lautenschlager et al., 2008; Sniehotta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference about the underlying assumption, supported by citations.

claim: Several studies, including one from our group, have failed to find a positive correlation between exercise-induced cognitive improvements and the associated physiological changes.
source: Despite the intuitive appeal of this assumption, several studies, including one from our group, have failed to find a positive correlation between exercise-induced cognitive improvements and the associated physiological changes (Moreau et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The absence of a clear link between the hypothesized physiological mechanisms of improvements and tangible cognitive gains might stem from the plurality and complexity of variables underlying these changes, rendering coherent associations elusive.
source: Arguably, the absence of a clear link between the hypothesized physiological mechanisms of improvements and tangible cognitive gains might stem from the plurality and complexity of variables underlying these changes, rendering coherent associations elusive.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of clear associations.

claim: The present study postulated that HIT would result in improvements in measures of cognitive control and working memory.
source: In the present study, we tested the viability of HIT as a substitute for aerobic exercise to induce cognitive improvements in school populations. In particular, we postulated that HIT would result in improvements in measures of cognitive control and working memory
evidence: This describes the hypothesis of the study.

claim: Both cognitive control and working memory have been linked to fitness levels.
source: In particular, we postulated that HIT would result in improvements in measures of cognitive control and working memory, as both constructs have been linked to fitness levels (Pontifex et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Both cognitive control and working memory appear to be malleable via aerobic regimens.
source: In particular, we postulated that HIT would result in improvements in measures of cognitive control and working memory, as both constructs have been linked to fitness levels (Pontifex et al., 2011) and appear to be malleable via aerobic regimens (Erickson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The choice of cognitive control and working memory constructs was motivated by previous research showing the malleability of both in training studies.
source: The choice of these constructs was also motivated by previous research showing the malleability of both cognitive control and working memory in training studies, thus providing theoretical and empirical support for the plausibility of expected improvements (Hampshire et al., 2012; Mishra et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study hypothesized that exercise training would elicit substantially larger cognitive benefits in individuals whose cardiovascular fitness is low.
source: Based on previous literature (Erickson et al., 2013; Moreau et al., 2015), we hypothesized that exercise training would elicit substantially larger cognitive benefits in individuals whose cardiovascular fitness is low
evidence: This describes a hypothesis of the study, supported by citations.

claim: The study hypothesized that exercise training would elicit substantially larger cognitive benefits in BDNF met66 carriers, whose activity-dependent BDNF levels are naturally limited.
source: Based on previous literature (Erickson et al., 2013; Moreau et al., 2015), we hypothesized that exercise training would elicit substantially larger cognitive benefits in individuals whose cardiovascular fitness is low, and in BDNF met66 carriers, whose activity-dependent BDNF levels are naturally limited.
evidence: This describes a hypothesis of the study, supported by citations.

claim: The study expected physiological improvements with exercise, as typically induced from aerobic interventions.
source: Finally, we expected physiological improvements with exercise, as typically induced from aerobic interventions (see for a review Gomez-Pinilla and Hillman, 2013).
evidence: This describes an expectation of the study, supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Participants in the exercise group saw a greater decrease in resting heart rate than controls.
source: Participants in the exercise group saw a greater decrease in resting heart rate than controls, as demonstrated by a Bayesian ANCOVA with Condition (HIT vs. Control) as a fixed factor and baseline heart rate as a covariate.
evidence: This is a result from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: The full model for resting heart rate change was preferred to the model with baseline resting heart rate only: BFM = 40.45.
source: The full model was preferred to the model with baseline resting heart rate only: BFM = 40.45
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: The full model for resting heart rate change was the most likely given the data: P(M | Data)=0.93.
source: The full model was preferred to the model with baseline resting heart rate only: BFM = 40.45, and was the most likely given our data: P(M | Data)=0.93
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: A Bayesian t-test on resting heart rate change showed a sizeable difference between the two groups, with larger gains for the HIT group (BF10 = 3.47).
source: Specifically, a Bayesian t-test on resting heart rate change showed a sizeable difference between the two groups, with larger gains for the HIT group (BF10 = 3.47, with Mgain = 6.11, SDgain = 11.64 and Mgain = 1.89, SDgain = 8.63, for HIT and Control, respectively; Hedges' g = 0.41 (0.09, 0.73).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Test-retest reliability for resting heart rate was acceptable (r = 0.77, BF10 = 1.75 e+51).
source: Test-retest reliability—assessed via a comparison between pretest and posttest resting heart rate for controls only—was acceptable (r = 0.77, BF10 = 1.75 e+51).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Participants did exercise at a suitable intensity overall, as expressed by the deviation from individual target heart rate values (MDev = 1.65, SDDev = 5.87).
source: Results showed that participants did exercise at a suitable intensity overall, as expressed by the deviation from individual target heart rate values (MDev = 1.65, SDDev = 5.87; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the study's analysis of workout intensity, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Effort intensity was maintained stable across time, as demonstrated by moderate evidence favoring the null model over an alternate model that included time as a predictor of maximum heart rate.
source: Importantly, effort intensity was maintained stable across time, as demonstrated by moderate evidence favoring the null model over an alternate model that included time as a predictor of maximum heart rate in a Bayesian linear regression analysis [BFM = 2.87, P(M | Data)=0.74, Figure 1C].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Individual resting heart rates tended to decrease throughout the intervention.
source: Because individual resting heart rates tended to decrease throughout the intervention, sustained effort indicates that individuals incrementally increased workout volume
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data.

claim: Individuals incrementally increased workout volume, as confirmed by additional measures such as step count.
source: Because individual resting heart rates tended to decrease throughout the intervention, sustained effort indicates that individuals incrementally increased workout volume, which was confirmed by additional measures such as step count [BFM = 2.979e + 10, P(M | Data) ≈ 1, for the model that included Session as a covariate, Figure 1D].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The intervention was adaptive, allowing workout intensities tailored to each individual.
source: Together, these results support the notion that the intervention was adaptive, allowing workout intensities tailored to each individual.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings about workout intensity and volume.

claim: An exploratory factor analysis using principal component extraction and promax rotation was performed on all six cognitive measures at pretest.
source: An exploratory factor analysis using principal component extraction and promax rotation was performed on all six cognitive measures at pretest.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used in the study.

claim: The scree plot and eigenvalues suggested a two-component solution for the cognitive measures.
source: The corresponding scree plot and eigenvalues (i.e. the variance in all variables accounted for by each factor) suggested a two-component solution (see factor loadings in Table 1 and Table 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a result from the exploratory factor analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Subsequent test of the two-factor model confirmed that the number of factors was sufficient (χ2 (4)=0.59, p=0.96; Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC = −22.05).
source: Subsequent test of the two-factor model confirmed that the number of factors was sufficient (χ2 (4)=0.59, p=0.96; Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC = −22.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: The two components extracted from the factor analysis are referred to as Cognitive Control and Working Memory.
source: We refer to these two components hereafter as Cognitive Control and Working Memory.
evidence: This describes the naming of the factors extracted in the analysis.

claim: The correlation between the Cognitive Control and Working Memory factors was r = 0.32.
source: The correlation between the two factors was r = 0.32.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA on Cognitive Control scores showed moderate evidence for the interaction model over the main effect model [BFM = 3.38, p(M | Data)=0.46].
source: A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA on Cognitive Control scores, with Session (pretest vs. posttest) as a within factor and Condition (HIT vs. Control) as a between factor, showed moderate evidence for the interaction model over the main effect model [BFM = 3.38, p(M | Data)=0.46; Table 2].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Participants in the HIT group showed larger improvements in Cognitive Control than controls from pretest to posttest (Mgain = 0.25, SDgain = 0.6 and Mgain = 0.08, SDgain = 0.47, respectively, Hedges' g = 0.31 [0.09, 0.54]).
source: Participants in the HIT group showed larger improvements than controls from pretest to posttest (Mgain = 0.25, SDgain = 0.6 and Mgain = 0.08, SDgain = 0.47, respectively, Hedges' g = 0.31 [0.09, 0.54]; Figure 2A, see also Figures 4–6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Figures 2A, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA on Working Memory scores showed strong evidence for the interaction model over the main effect model [BFM = 5233.68, p(M | Data) ≈1].
source: A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA on Working Memory scores, with Session (pretest vs. posttest) as a within factor and Condition (HIT vs. Control) as a between factor showed strong evidence for the interaction model over the main effect model [BFM = 5233.68, p(M | Data) ≈1; Table 3].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Table 3.

claim: Participants in the HIT group showed larger improvements in Working Memory than controls from pretest to posttest (Mgain = 0.48, SDgain = 0.83 and Mgain = 0.12, SDgain = 0.44, respectively, Hedges' g = 0.54 [0.31, 0.77]).
source: Participants in the HIT group showed larger improvements than controls from pretest to posttest (Mgain = 0.48, SDgain = 0.83 and Mgain = 0.12, SDgain = 0.44, respectively, Hedges' g = 0.54 [0.31, 0.77]; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A Bayesian regression analysis showed that change in resting heart rate was a reliable predictor of cognitive gains in Cognitive Control in the HIT group (BF10 = 6.34, p(M | Data)=0.86).
source: A Bayesian regression analysis showed that change in resting heart rate was a reliable predictor of cognitive gains in the HIT group, with respect to Cognitive Control (BF10 = 6.34, p(M | Data)=0.86).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Change in resting heart rate was not a reliable predictor of cognitive gains in Cognitive Control in the Control group (BF10 = 0.20, p(M | Data)=0.16).
source: This was not the case in the Control group (BF10 = 0.20, p(M | Data)=0.16).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: The contrast between HIT and Control groups was weaker when comparing Working Memory gains (HIT: BF10 = 0.56, p(M | Data)=0.36; Control: BF10 = 0.18, p(M | Data)=0.15).
